name: Math with Confidence
line: In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous. In Math with Confidence a parent teaches each lesson.
description: AMP vs Math with Confidence: in AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous. In Math with Confidence a parent teaches each lesson and judges each unit.
verdict: In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous. Every answer is checked and explained, updates the learner's level and sets the next problem. Math with Confidence is a K-6 print curriculum in which a parent teaches each lesson from a scripted guide, checks the workbook pages, and judges each unit at its Checkpoint [1][2].

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. Math with Confidence starts a child in the grade that matches their age, and the author lists the skills a grade assumes, for example grade 5 [1][4]. Each unit stays on one topic for several weeks [1][2]. Its checks come at the end of a unit: a Checkpoint that lists what the child should know, and from grade 3 a Unit Wrap-up [2].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Math with Confidence the unit is the lesson, taught by the parent from a scripted guide. In the early grades it is a warm-up and review, a few minutes of hands-on teaching with objects, then a short workbook page [1][2]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [5].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After every answer AMP shows whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps, before the next problem. In Math with Confidence the parent grades the workbook pages [2]. Across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, feedback that explains had the largest average effect [6]. These are averages by feedback type across ages and subjects, and effects were lower in primary and high school [6].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Math with Confidence keeps earlier skills fresh with warm-ups and spiral review [2]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed practice, which was also spaced, scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [7].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP an answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. A skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once, and repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. In Math with Confidence the parent reads the unit Checkpoint and decides whether to review or move on [2]. For weak facts, the author's grade 5 page suggests five minutes of daily practice [4].

rows.range: Kindergarten through grade 6, one grade at a time [1].
rows.start: No placement test found. The author advises the grade that matches the child's age, with a list of skills each grade assumes [1][4].
rows.teaching: A parent teaches each lesson from a scripted guide, with objects, games and picture books, then the child works a page [2][3].
rows.next: The next lesson in a fixed sequence of units. The parent decides whether to review or move on [2].
rows.mastery: Several weeks on each topic. A unit Checkpoint lists what the child should know, and the parent judges it [1][2].
rows.review: Warm-ups and spiral review to keep earlier skills fresh [2].
rows.print: Print or PDF is the whole program: a guide and one or two workbooks for each grade [1].
rows.adult: Teaches each lesson, gathers objects, prepares paper pieces and checks the workbook pages [2].
rows.reports: None built in. The parent grades, and Checkpoints and Unit Wrap-ups are the assessments [2].
rows.evidence: No entry in Evidence for ESSA. An author-run pilot has no comparison group [8][9].

theirs: Math with Confidence is a homeschool math curriculum for kindergarten through grade 6, written by Kate Snow and published by Well-Trained Mind Press [1][2]. Each grade has an Instructor Guide for the parent and a student workbook, in two parts from grade 3 [1]. The guide is scripted, so a parent can open it and teach [1].

A lesson is the parent and child together. In the early grades it starts with warm-up and review, then a few minutes of hands-on teaching, then a short workbook page. From grade 3 the parent leads the activities and the child then practices alone [2]. The teaching uses manipulatives, ten-frames, games, pretend play and picture-book suggestions [2][3]. Each unit stays on one topic for several weeks and ends with a Checkpoint [1][2].
credit: Hands-on teaching with objects, games and pretend play, with a parent at the table [2].
A scripted guide a parent can open and teach from [1].
Warm-ups and spiral review bring earlier skills back [2].

theirs: Math with Confidence has no entry in Evidence for ESSA [8]. We found no independent outcome study.

The author's pages report a pilot in which 75% of students "scored at the 98th or 99th percentile on a standardized test" [1][3]. The author's follow-up article gives the details: 77 fifth-grade students took the math section of the California Achievement Test online in spring 2024, and the author paid for the testing [9]. Scores are set against test norms, with no comparison group. The author calls it an informal survey, not a peer-reviewed study, and lists her own caveats: pilot families are committed and get extra support, they chose to take part, and other programs may do as well [9].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. Across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, feedback that explains had the largest average effect, 0.49, against 0.32 for the correct answer alone and 0.05 for right or wrong only. These are averages by feedback type, and effects were lower in primary and high school [6]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed practice, which was also spaced, scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [7]. AMP explains every answer and mixes its review into ordinary practice.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: You want to teach each math lesson yourself, at the table, with objects and games.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want every answer checked as it is given, with the worked steps.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice, set by your learner's own answers.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math, or past grade 6.
You want paper practice too, from workbooks made from your learner's own record.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Math with Confidence?
questions.answer: In Math with Confidence a parent teaches each lesson from a scripted guide, checks the pages, and judges each unit at its Checkpoint [1][2]. AMP has no separate test: every answer is checked, explained and sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Math with Confidence work?
questions.answer: We found no independent outcome study, and no entry in Evidence for ESSA [8]. The author reports an informal pilot of 77 fifth graders, scored against test norms, with no comparison group [9].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. A parent can keep teaching lessons from the book, and AMP places the learner from their first answers, whatever grade the book is in.
